title: Minimum Swaps to Avoid Forbidden Values
summary: Given two integer arrays, nums and forbidden, each of length n, you can swap any two distinct elements any number of times.
statement: Given two integer arrays, nums and forbidden, each of length n, you can swap any two distinct elements any number of times. Determine the minimum number of swaps required so that for every index i, the value of nums[i] does not match forbidden[i]. If it is impossible to achieve this, return -1.
constraints: nums and forbidden have equal length up to 100,000.
Any two distinct nums positions may be swapped in one operation.
Make nums[i] differ from forbidden[i] everywhere, or return -1 if impossible.
hints: Only positions currently equal to their forbidden value must be repaired, but global value capacity determines feasibility.
A swap fixes at most two bad positions; two bad positions can pair only when their values differ.
The answer is the larger of half the bad count rounded up and the largest bad-value frequency, after checking count(nums=v)+count(forbidden=v)≤n.
The two lower bounds are achievable by pairing different bad values first and using feasible helper positions for the remaining dominant value.
editorial: The two lower bounds are achievable by pairing different bad values first and using feasible helper positions for the remaining dominant value.

tests.explanation: Only the middle position conflicts; swapping values at positions one and two resolves it in one move.
Three copies of one cannot avoid the sole position that also forbids one, so return -1.
